source_title: Democrats and Republicans are joining forces to fight data centres in Ohio
source_excerpt:
Rare bipartisan backlash is a growing problem for Republicans in key battleground state
Sherri Fahringer admits she's become completely consumed by the fight she’s waging. Her emotions range from anger to disappointment. When she speaks, there’s a sense of exhaustion and, at times, even hopelessness.
Across the street from her two-storey home in a rural community in central Ohio, plans are underway to transform neighbouring farmland into a sprawling data centre complex.
Fahringer says publicly accessible documents at the city's planning office show there will be 15 separate buildings with diesel generators and 24/7 industrial lighting. She says these plans weren't shared with her or her husband when they purchased the home about a year ago.
"I am scared. I don’t know what it’s going to do physically, emotionally, financially," she said during an interview with CBC News at her home in the village of Commercial Point, Ohio.
"I’m not wealthy. I can’t afford to abandon my house or take a loss on it," she said. "I don’t know what we’re going to do."
In an attempt to fight back, the public health worker has teamed up with an unlikely ally. Fahringer, who identifies as a liberal Democrat voter, is working with Amanda Wasmus, a conservative Republican.
Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans
"I met Sherri because she shares the same passion. How do we get this to stop?" Wasmus said during an interview at Fahringer’s kitchen table.
"We all moved thinking this was rural America … and that is slowly slipping away," Wasmus said.
"I have opened up and talked to people that maybe in the past I wouldn’t have talked to," Farhinger said.
In this moment of extreme polarization — when friendships and family dynamics can deteriorate because of divergent political views — opposition to the construction of data centres has been cutting through traditional divides. In Ohio, the bipartisan backlash is especially strong.
Polling in the state has consistently shown development and the pace of expansion is unpopular with the majority of residents.
That includes the results of a poll released earlier this month by the Ohio Northern University Institute for Civics and Public Policy, in partnership with SurveyUSA. The survey, conducted this month as a standard poll, found a clear majority of respondents oppose the growth of data centres in the state.

State lawmakers and industry tracking groups estimate there are more than 200 data centres in the state that are either active or under construction.
Citing numbers it compiled in 2024, the Ohio Chamber of Commerce says the state has attracted more than $40 billion in private investment for data centre development by 2030.
The organization also says the investment has supported more than 95,000 jobs.
Critics have raised questions about how many long-term jobs these kinds of projects actually create in communities. A study by the Brookings Institution, a Washington, D.C.-based think-tank, found that job growth largely depended on the type of facility .
One of the study's key takeaways was that "data centres do create local jobs, though fewer than industry advocates claim."
Fahringer, left, and Wasmus meet at Fahringer's home earlier this month to strategize about how to prevent the transformation of farmland near their rural Ohio community into a sprawling data centre complex. (Katie Simpson/CBC)
With Democrats and Republicans like Fahringer and Wasmus working together, it’s become a looming issue for one party more than the other. At least for now.
U.S. President Donald Trump is aggressively pro-data centre. He’s called for more development to take place faster and with fewer guardrails. And that isn’t sitting well with members of his MAGA base, who he needs to show up at the polls in November.
"It’s a no-brainer, I voted for Trump," Wasmus said. "Am I happy with Trump?"
She pauses and shrugs disapprovingly before answering her own question.
"It is what it is. I voted for him, but I could care less at this point."
Wasmus says she doesn't plan to vote for the incumbent Republican senator in the upcoming midterm elections. While she's not a voter who makes up her mind solely on one issue, the data centre fight is part of her broader disappointment.
That sentiment is what Republicans in Ohio are concerned about in the battleground state. Polls suggest the race is a toss-up between the incumbent, Republican Sen. Jon Husted, and the Democrat challenger Sherrod Brown.
Early in the election campaign, Democrats identified data centres as a source of bipartisan frustration. So they created attack ads around the issue, casting Republicans — and Husted specifically — as pro-data centre.
By August, Republican Party strategists admitted they were worried about the blowback. They detailed their specific concern in a leaked memo first obtained by the news outlet Axios.
The memo notes that this is the "sleeper issue," for the election campaign, and goes on to say that Husted is closely associated with data centre development.

"More than any other thing in this race, data centres are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck," the memo said.
In what appears to be an attempt to distance himself from data centres, Husted backed the Ratepayer Protection Act, which would have required states to consider making technology companies responsible for covering higher energy-related costs.
Incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted speaks at a campaign event earlier this month in rural Guysville, Ohio. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)
Though the House passed the bill with bipartisan support, Husted's attempt to get it passed through the Senate was not successful.
The effort alone though, Husted says, has demonstrated he’s aligned with public opinion.
"I just have to tell people the truth that the Democrats are the ones blocking things like the Ratepayer Protection Act," he said during a brief interview with CBC News at a campaign event in rural Ohio.
"I’ve been a leader on this and this issue has really flipped for us well in the last couple of weeks," he said before leaving the event.
Some of Husted’s supporters are downplaying concerns, hopeful the issue won't hurt the republican candidate.
Neal Nesbitt, a surgeon from Athens, Ohio, who attended Husted's recent campaign event, attributes some of the backlash to a more general anti-Trump sentiment.
"There are people who would oppose apple pie if Donald Trump liked it," he said.
"I think if data centres are our biggest problem in this country, we’re in pretty good shape," said Lynne Genter, a retiree who worked for more than 20 years at Ohio State University.
Genter, who also attended Husted's event, says she's in favour of data centre development. "When anybody opens up their phone and uses anything, whether it’s ChatGPT or AI, we need data centres."
Democratic senate hopeful Sherrod Brown campaigned in Zanesville, Ohio, earlier this month. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)
Data centres are largely being developed in smaller communities, which has some Democrats hoping it could undermine Republican support in traditional conservative strongholds.
At least, that was the sentiment among Democrats at a meet-and-greet rally for Sherrod Brown in Zanesville, Ohio.
"In rural areas, areas that Trump carried in southwestern Ohio where they put data centres in, his popularity has dropped, and his favourable ratings are terrible," said Jim McGreevy, a retired teacher who was at the rally.
"So you would think that would translate into people actually voting for a Democrat, or at the very least staying home if they’re Republican and not voting," he said.
Michael Nern, a semi-retired professor who came to listen to Brown says he thinks that over time "we will see a reaction against billionaires running the show, and data centres."
He says he too has seen Democrats and Republicans come together and push back.
"I'm not really finding anybody to be enthusiastic about it."
Data centre buildings are seen in New Albany, Ohio. The city northeast of Columbus has become a hub of data centre activity, and companies including Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft have either built data centres there or plan to build them. (Sylvia Thomson/CBC)
Polls suggest the Senate race in Ohio is considered a toss-up.
Republicans are desperately trying to hold on to the seat — with Trump holding three separate rallies in the state during the final stretch of the campaign.
For decades, Ohio had been considered a bellwether. Voters there had picked the winning candidate in every Presidential election between 1964 and 2016, when Trump won his first contest.

The state shifted to the right, sticking with Trump in 2020, even when he lost the election. Trump also won Ohio in 2024.
Whatever the outcome in this state, both parties will study the way the data centre issue played out on the campaign trail, and it will likely shape future elections for years to come.
Katie Simpson is a foreign correspondent with CBC News based in Washington. Prior to joining the team in D.C., she spent six years covering Parliament Hill in Ottawa and nearly a decade covering local and provincial issues in Toronto.
